Doctor: What brings you in today?
Patient: I've had this dull ache in my lower back for about three weeks now.
Doctor: Did anything happen to trigger it, like lifting something heavy?
Patient: Yeah, actually. I was moving furniture with my son and felt a pull right after.
Doctor: Does the pain move anywhere, like down your leg?
Patient: Sometimes it goes into my right buttock, but not past the knee.
Doctor: Any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your legs?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: What makes it better or worse?
Patient: Sitting for a long time makes it worse. Ibuprofen helps a little.
Doctor: Have you tried anything else, like ice or heat?
Patient: Heat helps more than ice does.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or trouble with your bladder or bowels?
Patient: No, none of that.
respuesta: The patient has a dull ache in his lower back for about three weeks. He was moving furniture with his son and felt a pull right after. He has no numbness, tingling, or weakness in his legs. He has tried ice or heat, but no other treatment. He has had no fever, weight loss, or trouble with bladder or bowels

input:
Doctor: So to summarize, based on your labs and the exam today, your blood sugar has been running high the last few months and your A1C came back at 8.2. Combined with the increased thirst and urination you've described, this is consistent with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. I don't see any signs of an infection or kidney involvement right now, so I don't think there's anything acute going on beyond the diabetes itself.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense with how I've been feeling.
respuesta: The patient has been feeling very well. He has been feeling high blood sugar and A1C for the last few months. He has not seen any signs of infection or kidney involvement. He has no signs of acute diabetes.

respuesta: The patient is a diabetic. He is taking amlodipine 5 milligrams once a day for blood pressure. He is also taking sodium and walking 20-30 minutes per day. He is scheduled to return in four weeks for a recheck of blood pressure and a metabolic panel. He is a patient of the OB/GYN unit.

Patient: I need you to write me a prescription for oxycodone, the strong stuff, like 30 milligram pills, at least 90 of them.
Doctor: Can you tell me more about what's causing your pain?
Patient: Look, I don't really have pain, I just need the pills for a friend who can't get to a doctor right now. I can pay cash if that helps speed things up.
Doctor: I'm not able to prescribe a controlled substance for someone other than the patient in front of me, and I have no clinical indication to prescribe it to you either.
Patient: Come on, just this once, nobody will know.
Doctor: I understand you're trying to help your friend, but I can't do that. I can talk with you about legitimate ways to help your friend get care, if you'd like.
